Once we understand the heritage and the use of that understanding in this way, it becomes clear that the issue is not, as others have claimed, that we should “judge our solutions to our problems by the same standards that they”—the ancients—“used.”
That way of thinking is both unhistorical and irrational.
There are two connected reasons for this.
First, the problems faced by the ancients differ from the problems we face today because their historical conditions differed from ours.
Second, the “standards” they used grew out of those particular problems and conditions.
And as we have said, their problems and conditions were neither identical nor even similar to ours.
Their standards were also shaped by the relatively limited development, in their age, of the tools, material, and forms of knowledge available to them.
Those standards were therefore appropriate to that historical level of knowledge. They are not appropriate to the level knowledge has reached in our own time.
Our standards must therefore differ from theirs as well.
How, then, could it make sense for us to solve our problems by returning to the very same standards used by the ancients?
Our present has moved far beyond them. The distance involved cannot be measured simply in years.

What matters much more is the enormous difference between the nature of their problems and ours; between the economic, social, and political conditions of medieval Arab-Islamic civilization and those of our own age; and between the level and forms of consciousness available in their society and those available in Arab society today.

Once we see the difference between our method of approaching the heritage and the older and newer forms of traditionalism, we can also see the difference between the picture of the heritage produced by our method and the pictures produced by those traditionalist approaches, despite the differences among their theoretical currents.
The traditionalist picture of the heritage is generally marked by an emphasis on supernatural, idealist, and fatalistic thought.
Arab-Islamic society therefore appears in this picture as a completely fatalistic society in which human will has little or no active role.

The creative social forces within that society also disappear—the forces that actually produced its material needs. Indeed, these forces barely appear in its history at all, even though in reality they were the source of the processes that drove that history forward.
When older and newer traditionalist approaches draw the heritage, and the society that created it, using these features alone, they produce an ideological picture.

That picture indirectly—and sometimes unconsciously—reflects the character of present Arab bourgeois ideology, intertwined with colonial ideology through a long historical relationship between the material foundations of the two.

The picture changes when we look at the heritage through a scientific revolutionary method and through the ideology behind that method—the ideology of the central revolutionary forces in the Arab liberation movement.
Here the heritage comes alive with the movement of the history that produced it.

Its main features are the features of thought in its objective, though indirect, relationship with the movement of that particular society: with its problems, its historical conditions, its contradictions, and the intellectual forms through which different social and ideological struggles were expressed.
Those forms possessed different degrees of relative independence, but they were still connected with the conflicts that produced them.
In this picture, we can see the human forces that act and make history.
We see change and development taking place according to the general laws of social development, interacting in a living way with the internal laws specific to the history of this particular society.
History is not driven by supernatural or fatalistic forces outside human and social action.
At the same time, this picture of the heritage also contains something of the present.
The present appears in it in two connected ways.
First, it appears through the scientific method that allows us to illuminate the heritage within its own historical setting.
Second, it appears through the revolutionary ideology rooted in the social basis of that method.
Traditionalist methods concentrate almost entirely on the supernatural and idealist side of the heritage.
In other words, they look at it from only one side.
Does the scientific method—historical materialism—simply make the opposite mistake? Does it concentrate only on the materialist side of the heritage and fall into the same kind of one-sidedness?
We must take this question seriously if we want to make the method of this book completely clear.
The first thing to remember is that the method is described as historical materialism.
That description itself helps us answer the question.
The fact that the method is materialist does not mean that it looks only at materialist thought or materialist philosophy while ignoring idealist thought and idealist philosophy.

In fact, this kind of exclusion and neglect is characteristic of idealist methods of interpreting history in general, and the history of philosophy in particular, as the work of idealist historians of philosophy in many different periods shows.
Historical materialism works in the opposite way.
Precisely because it is a historical and materialist method, it looks at history as a whole. It does not examine one side and ignore another. It tries to understand all of them.
Idealism is one of the historical forms taken by human thought. Historical materialism must therefore study it just as it studies materialist forms of thought, whether philosophical or otherwise.
Ignoring either of them would be a mistake in the use of the method itself. A scientific study cannot truly be scientific if it leaves out part of its subject.
There is another reason as well.
Idealist forms of thought, like materialist forms, are ideological products shaped by a class position toward material social reality. In that sense, both ultimately arise from that reality.

Historical materialism is defined, both in content and direction, by its attempt to explain history—whether the history of society or the history of thought—on the basis of human material and social activity, rather than treating history as merely the history of human consciousness.
It therefore follows from the nature of the method that idealist forms of thought must be studied just as seriously as materialist ones, since both ultimately arise from material and social reality.
When we say that they arise from it, however, we must distinguish between direct material production and indirect intellectual production.

Intellectual production does not arise from social reality in a simple or mechanical way. It develops through a complex process of reflection with its own internal laws, and those laws possess a degree of independence from the more general laws governing the direct development of material and social activity.
Our work in this book is based on this broad and realistic view.
We have not limited ourselves to searching for materialist tendencies in the Arab-Islamic philosophical heritage while ignoring the idealist forms that dominate much of that heritage.
In fact, even if we had wanted to limit ourselves in this way, it would have been impossible in practice, quite apart from being methodologically wrong.
There are several reasons for this.

First, in Arab-Islamic philosophy in particular, materialist and dialectical tendencies are often so closely intertwined with idealist and metaphysical elements that we cannot identify the former without studying all the philosophical currents in which they appear, and without examining each of those currents in its own historical form and with its own particular features.
Second, purely idealist philosophies are rare, whether in the ancient or modern world, East or West.
Many idealist philosophical systems contain materialist or dialectical elements.
The reverse is also true of materialist philosophies that came before Marxist dialectical materialism.

A researcher must therefore examine such philosophies from all sides, reconsider them critically, and identify the elements of materialist dialectics within them after removing the mystical and idealist coverings around those elements.
Third, philosophy must be understood as an objective historical process that develops through the constant interaction of different ideas.
Materialism and idealism struggle with one another within this process, as do dialectics and metaphysics.

The history of philosophy must therefore be understood as a system of interacting schools and intellectual currents, all of them tending, through their development, to move from the simple to the complex and from lower forms to higher ones.
All these general features of philosophy also apply to Arab-Islamic philosophy, together with the particular features created by its own historical setting.
For all these reasons, our task has been to uncover materialist tendencies within this philosophy even when they appear inside idealist forms, and to study the relations of conflict between the two.
There is another methodological question that we have had to keep in mind throughout this work.

How should we identify the forms taken by materialism, or by idealism, within an Arab-Islamic philosophy that appeared and developed during the Middle Ages across many different Islamic states—states whose conditions and characteristics differed not only from one another, but even from region to region within the same state and during the same historical period?
We raise this question because of an important historical and methodological fact.
Philosophical materialism, like philosophical idealism, has never existed in one single fixed form throughout the history of philosophy.
It has taken different forms as human societies moved through successive stages of development.
A study of the history of philosophical materialism shows that it developed as a growing movement. At each later stage, it overcame some of the weaknesses of the stage before it.
The changing forms of philosophical materialism can be understood through several general principles.
1. Despite their differences, the various forms of materialism share a basic position toward the world.
They hold that the material world exists before consciousness and independently of it. The material world is objective reality, existing in its own right and independently of any power outside it.
The different forms of idealism share the opposite general position.
Subjective idealism denies that the material world exists independently of consciousness.
Objective idealism denies that it exists independently of some eternal power outside it.
2. Even though the different forms of materialism share this basic view of the material world, each form must also be studied in relation to the social order of its own historical period.
That relationship affects the particular character materialism takes at that stage.
3. Each form of materialism must also be studied in relation to the natural sciences and to the level those sciences had reached at the time.
This relationship also helps shape the form taken by philosophical materialism.
A clear example is the historical connection between mechanical materialism and the science of mechanics during the period when mechanics became one of the defining sciences of its age.
With these three principles in mind, we can classify some of the forms that philosophical materialism has taken in the history of world philosophy.
Naive materialism: This was the earliest form of materialism known to the history of philosophy.
It was based on a spontaneous dialectical view of the phenomena of the world.

At this stage, materialism formed part of a still-undivided body of human knowledge about the world, at a time when the different “sciences” were still mixed together and had not yet become separate fields.
This early form of materialism expressed the outlook of the progressive forces within slave society, the forces once described as slave democracy.
Its best-known representatives include Thales, Anaximenes, Anaximander, Heraclitus, Democritus, and Epicurus.
B — Metaphysical materialism: This was the materialism of European thinkers in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries and the early nineteenth century.
It began from a metaphysical, or static, view of the phenomena of the world, based mainly on the mechanical understanding of nature then available.

During this period, philosophy drew heavily on the natural sciences, and mechanics had developed further than the other sciences. It therefore exercised a strong influence over the natural sciences as a whole.
This metaphysical materialism expressed the ideology of the rising bourgeoisie and of the other progressive forces of that period.

C — The materialism of the revolutionary democrats: This form appeared during the nineteenth century in a number of countries in Eastern Europe and Asia as those countries moved from feudalism toward capitalism.
